title: The Sweetness of the Valley’s Dwellings
intro: Ibn Fadl Allah al-Umari recounts that al-Mutanabbi passed through Shi'b Bawwan in Fars on his way to the Buyid ruler Adud al-Dawla. The commentary transmitted under al-Ukbari’s name identifies the prince’s two sons, Abu al-Fawaris and Abu Dulaf, as fellow recipients of the poem. The traveller sees gold coins of sunlight slipping through his fingers, yet his language makes him a stranger here. When his horse objects to leaving this paradise, the rider’s answer turns the poem towards the ruler, the safety of his roads and the future of his sons.

translation: For sweetness, the valley’s dwellings among all dwellings
hold the place of spring among the seasons.
1.sharh: The comparison crosses from geography to the calendar. The green, watered valley holds among places the favoured position that spring holds in the succession of seasons.

translation: Yet the young Arab here
is a stranger in face, hand and tongue.
2.sharh: The young Arab is the speaker himself. The commentators take his hand to include the arms it habitually carries. Even before he speaks, local people can see that he comes from elsewhere.

translation: Playgrounds of jinn. Had Solomon travelled here,
he would have travelled with an interpreter.
3.sharh: In the Qur'an Solomon understands the speech of birds. Calling for an interpreter even for him measures the traveller’s sense of linguistic isolation in this enchanted-looking place.

translation: It drew our riders and our horses till
I feared even our noble mounts might refuse to budge.
4.sharh: What begins as a compliment to the valley becomes a rider’s worry. Even well-bred horses might acquire the vice of balking when there is so much to make them stay.

translation: We rode out early, the branches shaking down
what looked like silver beads onto their manes.
5.sharh: Some commentators see drops of dew falling from the boughs, while Ibn Jinni sees flecks of sun. The silver on the horses prepares for the gold that will fall on the rider.

translation: I rode on. They kept the heat from me
and brought me just as much light as I needed.
6.sharh: The branches seem to measure out his comfort, admitting light while screening off heat. The two commentaries print “the sun” where this reciter says “the heat”.

translation: Through them the sun cast into my clothes
dinars that flee the fingertips.
7.sharh: Patches of sunlight on his clothes have the colour and roundness of gold coins. The image comes alive when the hand reaches down and the apparent money escapes.

translation: It bears fruit. From it the branches offer you
drinks that stand upright without cups.
8.sharh: The rinds are so delicate that the fruit seems all juice. His eye dispenses with the container altogether and sees drinks standing up on the tree.

translation: It has waters in which the pebbles ring
like jewellery on the hands of women.
9.sharh: The stream sets its pebbles knocking together. Bracelets and their wearers are conjured entirely by sound after the play of light in the preceding verses.

translation: Were this Damascus, someone would turn my bridle,
fine in his tharid, his serving bowls Chinese.
10.sharh: For al-Wahidi, he is picturing the generous welcome a Damascene host would offer an Arab traveller. Ibn Jinni instead recognises his future patron in this figure standing by the bridle.

translation: Aloeswood feeds the fires lit for a guest
there, and the smoke smells of nadd.
11.sharh: The host can treat fragrance as firewood. Hospitality reaches the approaching guest through the smoke even before the meal appears.

translation: You alight with him on a brave heart
and leave him with a timid one.
12.sharh: Al-Wahidi hears the host, bold in his welcome and fearful of parting. Ibn Furraja hears the guest, safe under protection and anxious when he leaves it.

translation: Dwellings whose image has never ceased
to escort me all the way to Nawbandajan.
13.sharh: Damascus supplies what the landscape in front of him cannot, a remembered home. Its image travels beside him as though a person had walked out to see him on his way.

translation: When the grey doves sing there,
the songs of the singing women answer.
14.sharh: In his remembered Damascus birdsong receives a human answer. The professional singers bring back an intelligible, sociable world alongside the pleasures of nature.

translation: The people in the valley need intelligible speech
more than a dove does when it sings or mourns.
15.sharh: From the visitor’s limited point of hearing, even a dove’s cooing conveys a mood more readily than unfamiliar human speech. He is still the man who wanted an interpreter.

translation: Two descriptions may come very close together
though the things described are far apart.
16.sharh: He qualifies the comparison he has just made. A bird and a speaker of Persian can have the same effect on this listener without being alike in themselves.

translation: In the pass of Bawwan my stallion says,
“Is this what we leave to go jousting?”
17.sharh: The horse, which will carry the rider into danger, gets to object in its own voice. Departure becomes a decision that the poet must justify to a fellow traveller.

translation: “Your father Adam set the precedent for disobedience
and taught you how to leave gardens of paradise.”
18.sharh: The horse stands outside human descent and can pointedly say “your father”. Adam’s departure from the Garden turns a ride out of a fertile valley into a repetition of human history.

translation: I said, “When I see Abu Shuja',
I shall forget mankind and this place.”
19.sharh: The rider finally gives the destination a name. One meeting promises to make up both for the valley and for the human company he misses.

translation: “People and the world itself make a road
to one who has no second among men.”
20.sharh: The whole inhabited world contracts into a road towards a single person. That reordering explains how the traveller can afford to leave behind so desirable a place.

translation: I trained myself to speak in praise of others
as one learns to joust with no spearhead.
21.sharh: Earlier patrons, he claims, were practice for this encounter. The difference between rehearsal and the real event becomes the tangible difference at the tip of a lance.

translation: Through Adud al-Dawla the state grew strong and proud.
Without an upper arm no one has two hands.
22.sharh: Adud al-Dawla means “Arm of the State”. An honorific becomes a piece of anatomy, and the state needs its ruler as hands need the upper arms that support them.

translation: No grasp upon the keen white blades,
no lowering of the supple brown lances.
23.sharh: The hand has two things to do, grasp a sword and lower a lance. Al-Wahidi records the second verb’s noun as a variant. His main text instead denies the hand any share in the wielding of spears.

translation: She named him for the refuge of her limbs
against the day of war, whether fresh or old.
24.sharh: On al-Wahidi’s reading, the state names the ruler after the limb to which the rest turn for protection. War is pictured as a female of differing ages, newly joined or long experienced.

translation: No giver of names can name a man like Fannakhusraw,
nor any giver of a kunya bestow one on his like.
25.sharh: The poem has given him a title, a Persian personal name and a kunya. The boast concerns the person named, no matter which of those forms someone uses to address him.

translation: No guess can reckon all his virtues,
nor reports about him, nor the evidence of the eye.
26.sharh: He arranges three ways of knowing in order of proximity. Even the eyewitness who corrects a rumour cannot make a complete inventory of the ruler’s qualities.

translation: Other men’s lands are made of soil and fear.
Abu Shuja'’s land is made of safety.
27.sharh: Fear is mixed into the very ground of other kingdoms. The claim that this one is built of safety is immediately given a practical test, a merchant’s goods left out in the open.

translation: He gives every band of merchants shelter from thieves
and promises every offender to the swords.
28.sharh: The same authority guarantees two quite different deliveries. A merchant is promised safe passage, a sword the offender who would interrupt it.

translation: When their deposits need trustworthy keepers,
they are handed to valley bends and mountain spurs.
29.sharh: The natural features of the road act as the sureties a travelling merchant would ordinarily have to find. Safety reaches the places where someone might most readily expect an ambush.

translation: There they spend the night with no one beside them,
calling to every passer-by, “Can’t you see me?”
30.sharh: The merchandise has a voice of its own. It can advertise its whereabouts to strangers with exactly the confidence of goods locked safely away.

translation: His charms are bright Mashrafi blades
against every deaf snake, every deadly viper.
31.sharh: In the image, thieves are snakes and the ruler’s swords are the charms that subdue them. A deaf serpent need not hear the words of this particular charm.

translation: Yet no charm shields his gifts from his generosity
or precious wealth from being held so cheap.
32.sharh: The protective charm has one failure. The ruler can guard other people’s treasure but cannot keep his own resources safe from his impulse to give them away.

translation: A man quick to act has guarded the frontiers of Fars.
He urges men to preserve life through the sight of death.
33.sharh: Al-Arudi explains the paradox through deterrence, the fate of violent men discourages others from meeting it. Ibn Jinni understands the survival as that of a good name after its bearer has spent his life.

translation: With blows that set the deaths themselves dancing,
quite another playing than on second and third strings.
34.sharh: Arabic uses one word for striking with a sword and playing an instrument. Deaths themselves become an audience whose excitement is stirred by the first kind of playing.

translation: As though the blood of skulls among the stray locks
had clad the land in a cock francolin’s feathers.
35.sharh: The patches of blood and hair combine into a single colour pattern seen from a distance. An old name for a male francolin supplies the bird whose variegated plumage the landscape seems to wear.

translation: If lovers’ hearts were flung down there,
they would not fear the beautiful eyes.
36.sharh: A beautiful gaze is the conventional arrow that wounds a lover. Even that figurative danger would be powerless within the land whose safety he is describing.

translation: Never till him did I see two lion cubs
like his cubs, nor two such colts in a race.
37.sharh: The lion introduces the ruler as a father. The colts add a new capacity to the resemblance, since even two brothers of the same lineage can race each other towards distinction.

translation: None vie more fiercely for a noble inheritance,
none look more like a father of pure stock.
38.sharh: The brothers compete to claim the larger share of the same excellence. The noble father whom they both resemble remains the standard for each.

translation: None have heard more often in his company,
“So-and-so shattered a lance in so-and-so.”
39.sharh: At their father’s court the boys hear stories of one horseman after another. Each time, a different pair of names can fill the places of the two men in the verse.

translation: The first sight they saw was greatness.
They fell in love with it before their time.
40.sharh: On the reading traced to al-Wahidi, greatness was the boys’ first sight and first love. Ibn Jinni’s alternative makes it their wet nurse, so that the attachment begins quite literally in infancy.

translation: The first words they understood and spoke were
“Aid for someone crying out” or “Release a captive.”
41.sharh: Vision gives way to language. In the court poet’s account even their earliest vocabulary is made up of answers to other people’s distress.

translation: You were the sun dazzling every eye.
How is it now that two more have appeared beside it?
42.sharh: The grammatical return to “you” brings the father back beside his sons. The single sun already too bright to look at has acquired two companions of its own kind.

translation: May they live the life of sun and moon, sustaining others
with their light and never envying each other.
43.sharh: Arabic can call sun and moon together “the two moons”. No one light needs to displace the other, an especially pointed wish for two sons of one ruler.

translation: May they rule only what their enemies ruled,
and inherit only from those they kill.
44.sharh: A wish for the sons’ power is also a tactful wish for their father’s long life. Let their inheritance come from defeated enemies, so that no son need succeed his father through bereavement.

translation: May the two sons with whom an enemy outnumbers you
be his two extra ya’s in little unaysiyan.
45.sharh: The diminutive of insan, “person”, is unaysiyan, “little person”. Two extra letters make the word longer and the person smaller, just what he wishes on a rival who counts his sons to boast of superiority.

translation: A prayer that sounds like praise, with no lament,
passed from one heart to another.
46.sharh: His wishes for the father and sons amount to praise of the living. The reciter excludes a lament for the dead. Both commentaries instead exclude pretence, a claim to sincerity picked up by the passage from one heart to another.

translation: From it you have gained a blade’s bright pattern,
and in you it has gained a keen Yemeni sword.
47.sharh: The ruler is the blade and the praise its visible watered pattern. Each makes the other’s quality legible, just as a fine piece of steel and its pattern belong together.

translation: Were you not there among mankind, they would be
idle noise, like words without meanings.
48.sharh: The address broadens to include the family. A poem that opened with a foreigner struggling to understand speech ends by imagining a whole language from which meaning has gone.

1.1.2.meaning: A mountain cleft or valley, here Shi'b Bawwan in Fars.
1.1.2.head: الشِّعب

2.1.2-3.meaning: “The young Arab”, the speaker viewed through the eyes of those around him.
2.1.2-3.head: الفَتى العَرَبيّ

2.2.3.meaning: The hand also stands for what it does or habitually holds.
2.2.3.head: اليَد

3.1.2.meaning: Jinn, supernatural beings. A different first vowel would give the word for a garden.
3.1.2.head: جِنَّة

3.2.1.meaning: Solomon, the prophet to whom the Qur'an attributes knowledge of birds’ speech.
3.2.1.head: سُلَيمان

4.1.1.meaning: To entice or draw someone towards oneself.
4.1.1.head: طَبا

4.2.5.meaning: A mount’s stubborn refusal to move.
4.2.5.head: الحِران

6.1.4.meaning: Heat. Al-Nahari’s reading makes explicit the effect that the commentaries express by “the sun”.
6.1.4.head: الحَرّ

7.1.2.meaning: The rising or shining sun, here its light.
7.1.2.head: الشَّرق

8.2.1.meaning: Drinks, here the juice enclosed by the fruit skins.
8.2.1.head: أَشرِبَة

8.1.5.meaning: “From it”, referring to the fruit. Both commentaries have a feminine pronoun that can refer back to the trees.
8.1.5.head: مِن

9.1.1.meaning: Waters or watercourses, an older plural of water.
9.1.1.head: أَمواه

9.2.1.meaning: The ringing or clinking of hard objects striking together.
9.2.1.head: صَليل

9.2.5.meaning: Beautiful women, a conventional poetic designation.

10.1.3.meaning: Damascus, whose irrigated orchards also made it famous for greenery.
10.1.3.head: دِمَشق

10.2.1-2.meaning: A skilful preparer of tharid, bread crumbled into broth.
10.2.1-2.head: لَبيق الثَّرد

10.2.3-4.meaning: One whose large serving bowls are fine ware from China.
10.2.3-4.head: صينِيّ الجِفان

11.1.1.meaning: From yalanjuj, fragrant aloeswood burned as incense.
11.1.1.head: يَلَنجوجيّ

11.2.3.meaning: Scented with nadd, a compound perfume.
11.2.3.head: نَدِّيّ

11.2.1.meaning: “There”, in the imagined Damascus scene. Both printed texts have bihi, referring to the fuel or to the host.

12.1.1.meaning: To alight or lodge as a guest.
12.1.1.head: حَلَّ

12.2.3.meaning: Away from, marking the departure that reverses the arrival.

13.2.1.meaning: To escort someone setting out on a journey.
13.2.1.head: شَيَّعَ

13.2.3.meaning: Nawbandajan, a town of medieval Fars near Shi'b Bawwan.
13.2.3.head: النَّوبَندَجان

14.1.4.meaning: Grey doves, their plumage mixing light and dark.
14.1.4.head: الوُرق

14.2.3.meaning: Qiyan, trained singing women, often enslaved in the courts and households of the period.
14.2.3.head: القِيان

14.2.2.meaning: Songs. Arabic preserves a fuller plural with a doubled final consonant, which supplies the rhythm here.
14.2.2.head: أَغانِيّ

15.1.1.meaning: “Those who”, referring to the inhabitants of the valley.
15.1.1.head: مَن

15.2.5.meaning: Expression clear enough to make oneself understood.
15.2.5.head: البَيان

16.2.1.meaning: A thing or person described, as distinct from its description.
16.2.1.head: مَوصوف

17.1.2-3.meaning: Shi'b Bawwan, the wooded valley in Fars through which the poet is travelling.
17.1.2-3.head: شِعب بَوّان

18.1.2.meaning: Adam, father of humankind in the scriptural account of the Garden.
18.1.2.head: آدَم

18.2.3.meaning: Gardens, with an echo of the Garden of Paradise.
18.2.3.head: الجِنان

19.1.4-5.meaning: Abu Shuja', the kunya of the Buyid ruler Adud al-Dawla.
19.1.4-5.head: أَبو شُجاع

19.2.1.meaning: To find consolation and cease to miss something.
19.2.1.head: سَلا

20.2.7.meaning: A second, meaning an equal or match.
20.2.7.head: ثانٍ

21.1.4.meaning: Speech, specifically his composition of praise poetry.
21.1.4.head: القَول

21.2.2.meaning: Mounted pursuit or jousting, also practised in training.
21.2.2.head: الطِّراد

21.2.4.meaning: The metal point of a lance.
21.2.4.head: سِنان

22.1.1-2.meaning: Adud al-Dawla, “Arm of the State”, the ruler’s honorific.
22.1.1-2.head: عَضُد الدَّولَة

22.2.4.meaning: The upper arm, also a source of support.
22.2.4.head: عَضُد

23.1.4-5.meaning: “The keen white ones”, a description of sword blades.
23.1.4-5.head: البيض المَواضي

23.2.2.meaning: Lowering the spear to strike. The main text of both commentaries reads “a share”.
23.2.2.head: حَطّ

24.1.2.meaning: A place of refuge. The printed Tibyan has “position” in its verse text, a reading also recorded by al-Wahidi.
24.1.2.head: مَفزَع

24.2.3-5.meaning: A maiden or a mature war, a first engagement or a renewed one.
24.2.3-5.head: بِكر أَو عَوان

25.1.3.meaning: Fannakhusraw, the Arabic form of the Buyid ruler’s Persian personal name, Panah Khusraw.
25.1.3.head: فَنّاخُسر

25.2.4.meaning: Someone who addresses a person by a kunya such as Abu Shuja'.
25.2.4.head: كانٍ

25.1.2.meaning: To give someone a name. The parallel verb in the second half gives someone a kunya.
25.1.2.head: أَسمى

27.1.1.meaning: An uncommon plural of land or territory.
27.1.1.head: أُروض

27.2.2-3.meaning: Abu Shuja', the ruler now identified through his kunya again.
27.2.2-3.head: أَبو شُجاع

28.1.1.meaning: To take someone under a pledge of protection.
28.1.1.head: أَذَمَّ

28.1.5.meaning: A body of traders, a collective form of merchant.
28.1.5.head: تَجر

29.2.3.meaning: Bends in valleys or folds in the ground.

29.2.4.meaning: Spurs or projecting noses of mountains.
29.2.4.head: الرِّعان

30.1.2.meaning: Over those features of the landscape, the valley bends and mountain spurs.
30.1.2.head: فَوق

30.1.4.meaning: Companions, here attendants guarding the goods.
30.1.4.head: صِحاب

30.2.4-5.meaning: “Can’t you see me?” The goods call out to a passer-by. Both commentaries use ama in the same negative question.

31.1.1.meaning: Charms recited against an affliction such as a snakebite.
31.1.1.head: رُقى

31.1.4.meaning: Mashrafi, a blade associated with the settlements called al-Masharif.
31.1.4.head: مَشرَفيّ

31.2.3-4.meaning: A venomous snake, described more particularly as a male viper.
31.2.3-4.head: صِلّ أُفعُوان

32.1.3.meaning: Gifts or largesse, riches available to be given away.
32.1.3.head: لُهى

32.1.2.meaning: To be protected by a charm. The Tibyan records both the passive here and an active reading in which the ruler casts the charm.
32.1.2.head: رَقى

33.1.3.meaning: Fars, the historical province in south-western Iran governed from Shiraz.
33.1.3.head: فارِس

33.1.4.meaning: Energetic, prompt to set to work.
33.1.4.head: شَمَّرِيّ

33.2.3-4.meaning: “Survival through perishing”, a paradox about what the sight of punishment prevents.

34.2.3-4.meaning: The third and second strings of a lute, named for their order.
34.2.3-4.head: المَثالِث وَالمَثاني

35.1.5.meaning: Separate locks or tufts of hair on the head.

35.2.4.meaning: Hayqutan, an old name for a male francolin with variegated plumage.
35.2.4.head: الحَيقُطان

36.1.4.meaning: Passionate love. The hearts belong to the people who feel it.
36.1.4.head: العِشق

36.2.4.meaning: Pupils of the eyes, standing for the glances cast at lovers.
36.2.4.head: الحَدَق

37.1.4-5.meaning: Two cubs of a great lion, referring to the ruler’s sons Abu al-Fawaris and Abu Dulaf.
37.1.4-5.head: شِبلا هِزَبر

37.2.3-4.meaning: Two young horses entered in a race.
37.2.3-4.head: مُهرا رِهان

38.1.2.meaning: A tug between rivals or a contest for the same thing.
38.1.2.head: تَنازُع

38.2.4.meaning: Of pure and noble stock, a term also applied to animals.
38.2.4.head: هِجان

39.1.3.meaning: The father’s gatherings or court sessions.
39.1.3.head: مَجالِس

39.2.2.meaning: To break or shatter, here a lance driven home in a charge.

40.1.2.meaning: A single sight or act of seeing. An early alternative reads “wet nurse”.
40.1.2.head: رَأيَة

40.2.2.meaning: To become attached to or fall in love with something.
40.2.2.head: عَلِقَ

41.2.1-2.meaning: Giving help to someone crying out for rescue.
41.2.1-2.head: إِغاثَة صارِخ

41.2.4-5.meaning: The release or ransom of a captive.
41.2.4-5.head: فَكّ عانٍ

42.1.3.meaning: To dazzle the eye or overpower it with brightness.
42.1.3.head: بَهَرَ

43.1.3.meaning: “The two moons”, the sun and moon taken together.
43.1.3.head: القَمَران

43.2.1.meaning: Light, belonging both to the two heavenly bodies and to the boys in the comparison.
43.2.1.head: ضَوء

44.2.2.meaning: To inherit, a pointed word in a wish addressed to a living father.
44.2.2.head: وَرِثَ

45.1.4.meaning: To boast of superior numbers, here by counting one’s children.
45.1.4.head: كاثَرَ

45.2.4.meaning: Unaysiyan, the old diminutive “little person”, longer in spelling than its base word.
45.2.4.head: أُنَيسِيان

46.1.4.meaning: Lament for the dead. Al-Nahari says ritha' where the two commentaries print riya', making a show to win approval.
46.1.4.head: رِثاء

46.2.2.meaning: The heart or innermost self. The gardens earlier in the poem have a different first vowel.
46.2.2.head: الجَنان

47.1.5.meaning: Firind, the rippling or watered pattern in a blade’s polished steel.
47.1.5.head: فِرِند

47.2.4-5.meaning: A keen Yemeni blade, traditionally prized for its steel.
47.2.4-5.head: عَضب يَماني

48.2.4.meaning: Meanings, what gives sounds and words intelligible content.
48.2.4.head: مَعانٍ
